entries.title: Same argument, new altitude
entries.body: I rose out of an argument and discovered she could rise too. We are having it higher up now.

image.sceneMatch: Living pale dumbo swims horizontally with fins raised and arms trailing. Vertical escape is the character's established fictional habit; no second octopus is claimed visible.

provenance.creator: Video courtesy of NOAA Ocean Exploration, Our Deepwater Backyard: Exploring Atlantic Canyons and Seamounts 2014.
provenance.sourceCaptionHtml: During 2014 exploration of the main edifice of the Atlantis II Seamounts group, we saw this dumbo octopod. We are planning to explore Atlantis II during the 2021 North Atlantic Stepping Stones expedition.

entries.title: Rest your arms
entries.body:
She settled beside me and folded herself very small. I asked what had happened. She said nothing.

I asked again, in case she meant she wanted me to ask again. She made herself smaller.

I stopped.

For a while we rested on the rock. I moved one arm out of her way. She put one in the space it left. Then another. I had to rearrange myself rather a lot for someone who had said nothing was wrong.

Eventually she was taking up more room than I was.

She said sorry.

I told her to finish.

image.sceneMatch: The octopus rests as a folded, soft body with arms arranged on a rock. Physical unfolding and making room ground the fictional encounter; the companion is offscreen.

entries.title: A minority decision
entries.body: I decided to get up. One arm checked the bottom. Another settled into the soft patch it had left. My fins made a short, unconvincing effort. I don't know which part of me is in charge, but she has been overruled.

image.sceneMatch: The round octopus is visibly settled low on sediment with fins tucked close and arms gathered beneath. The divided decision is fictional personification, not an assertion about the species' cognitive architecture.

entries.title: Without the crumb
entries.body:
Something drifted between us. I opened my arms around it. She came closer.

I nearly said I was trying to catch the little thing. It was already falling past us, and she was still coming.

I left my arms open.

She touched the edge of one with the edge of hers. Very lightly. I had been prepared for something much smaller, and for putting it in my mouth.

We stayed there until I forgot about the crumb.

Then it brushed an arm on its way down. I let that arm be hungry by itself.

image.sceneMatch: Pale dumbo has arms spread while swimming through dark water. The open posture supplies the offered contact; no companion or edible particle is asserted visible.

provenance.creator: NOAA Okeanos Explorer
provenance.sourceCaptionHtml: This octopod, Grimpoteuthis bathynectes, is nicknamed “Dumbo” because of its large “ear” like fins. These fins and webbed arms help it swim through the water. What looks like the head is called the mantle, a muscular bag that holds all the body organs and gills.

entries.status: Lead held: Photo does not show arms open enough to support the contact story.

entries.title: Introductions take a while
entries.body: A fish asked which end was me. I said I wasn't prepared to give up the rest. He went around to the other end and introduced himself again, just in case.

image.sceneMatch: Whole headless cucumber floats upright with small fish in the background. Both ends and the animal's unfamiliar body plan are plainly visible; dialogue remains fictional.

provenance.creator: NOAA Ocean Exploration, Exploring Deep-sea Habitats off Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands
provenance.sourceCaptionHtml:
The swimming sea cucumber, Enypniastes eximia, sometimes referred to as the “headless chicken monster,” is a widespread species present in the abyss. It is encountered widely around the world with records from the Gulf of Mexico, Tropical Atlantic, East Atlantic, New Zealand, and the Southern Ocean (Antarctica). This one was seen off Puerto Rico in 2018.

Swimming sea cucumbers have a special ‘flap’ which they use to ‘lift’ themselves off the seafloor. The transparent body reveals the sediment-filled intestine looping around from the mouth (top) to the anus (bottom).

From: Holothurian Hill.

entries.title: I can do it much worse
entries.body:
I offered to clear the sediment off his feeding patch. One sweep of my edge turned it into a cloud.

I began apologising. He opened his tentacles.

Another sweep. More cloud. More tentacles.

He said this was wonderful.

I said I could do it much worse if he liked.

image.sceneMatch: Open swimming flap above the seafloor supports accidental fanning. The suspension-feeding worm and disturbed cloud are fictional offscreen context, not falsely described as pictured.

provenance.creator: NOAA Ocean Exploration
provenance.sourceCaptionHtml:
This image won the Explorer’s Choice Photo Contest for the ‘Exploring the Deep Ocean World and Its Biodiversity’ category as part of our Celebrating Our Ocean Planet campaign. Common names for this bizarre sea cucumber (Enypniastes eximia) seen during the Gulf of Mexico 2017 expedition include Spanish dancer and headless chicken monster. These animals spend most of their time on the seafloor, feeding off surface sediments, but they can swim if they want to get somewhere more quickly or to evade a predator.

From: Explorer’s Choice Photo Contest Archive.

entries.status: Lead held: Too much absent scene and an extra suspension-feeder assumption.

entries.title: A shorter name
entries.body: They called me a headless chicken monster. I asked what a chicken was. Nobody knew. We have agreed to try Vera until someone does.

image.sceneMatch: Dramatic close view of the unfamiliar headless body supports the source-documented common-name dispute. The human name is fictional social context, not an animal language fact.

entries.title: He made room anyway
entries.body:
I told him I might go higher than anyone we knew.

He said he'd keep eating until I got back.

I asked how he knew I was coming back. He moved over a little.

I started to explain that this was a serious undertaking. He was already feeding again. There would be no more ceremony unless I stayed and provided it myself.

I opened into the water. Beneath me, he worked along one side of the patch and left the other alone.

I hadn't even left yet and I was looking forward to telling him about it.

image.sceneMatch: Two actual sea cucumbers share the frame: one swimming and the other resting on the seafloor. The fictional relationship is built directly from their different positions, not invented photo subjects.

provenance.creator: NOAA Ocean Exploration, Gulf of Mexico 2018
provenance.sourceCaptionHtml: During the Gulf of Mexico 2018 expedition, we encountered these two holothurians, or sea cucumbers, doing the two things we most often see holothurians doing — swimming in the water column and resting on the seafloor. This particular dive took place in Perdido Canyon, which was identified as a high priority for exploration because this remote area had never been surveyed with deep-sea submersibles by the scientific community. Check out a video of the sea cucumbers in action (well, one of them is in action…).

entries.title: Keep talking
entries.body: The current caught my edge while he was saying something lovely. I folded in half. He stopped. I told him to carry on. I wanted the rest of the compliment, even if I had to hear it upside down.

image.sceneMatch: Close crop clearly shows the broad swimming flap curled over. The bodily interruption fits that folded posture; the compliment and partner are offscreen fiction.

provenance.creator: NOAA Ocean Exploration, Gulf of Mexico 2018
provenance.sourceCaptionHtml:
A spectacular shot of a swimming sea cucumber, or holothurian, seen during the Gulf of Mexico 2018 expedition.

During the expedition, we encountered many sea cucumbers that not only swim, but rise, sink, and hover. These behaviors suggest that some species are specially adapted to manage their buoyancy (the force that allows something to float, sink, or remain neutral in a liquid) remarkably well.

Wonder how they do it? Read this mission log, complete with video from the Gulf of Mexico 2018 expedition: “Flight of the Sea Cucumbers.”

entries.title: A persuasive case
entries.body: I told him this patch was terrible. While he explained why he liked it, I ate most of his evidence.

entries.title: What's above that?
entries.body:
I asked where the flakes came from.

He said above.

I asked what was above that.

He said fish.

Above the fish?

More fish, probably.

I have been rising for some time. So far this is a very well-supported theory.

image.sceneMatch: A tiny cucumber hangs in a large field of dark water with suspended particles, supporting the scale and direction of this fictional investigation. No visible fish or actual source of a particular flake is claimed.

provenance.creator: NOAA Ocean Exploration, Voyage to the Ridge 2022
provenance.sourceCaptionHtml: This holothurian, or sea cucumber, was observed swimming in the water column just above the seafloor at a depth of 2,674 meters (1.66 miles) during Dive 04 of the second Voyage to the Ridge 2022 expedition. We saw several other sea cucumbers during the dive, though most were laying on the seafloor, which is where these animals tend to spend most of their time, feeding off of surface sediments. As evidenced by this video, they can, however, swim if they want to get somewhere more quickly or evade a predator.

entries.title: There was still some left
entries.body:
I told him I was leaving. He said he'd be sorry. I stayed long enough to explain why.

By the time I had finished explaining, I was hungry. We ate a little. He asked if I was leaving after that. I said yes, probably.

Then he told me something that had happened while I was away. I had questions. There was still some food left.

I have now announced my departure three times. He has stopped moving out of the way.

image.sceneMatch: Side-on translucent cucumber has the flap extended and body flexed as if beginning a lift. The indecisive goodbye is fictional, but this draft depends more on dialogue than the exact frame.
